The Independent (independent.co.uk), by Maroosha Muzaffar — "Japan says it's time for 'taboo-free' discussions about acquiring nuclear weapons". Published Wednesday 30 September 2026, 10:35 BST. CONFIRMED 30 Sep.
Retrieved via Exa search snippet (WebFetch blocked on independent.co.uk from this environment). Text below is the article's own words as returned.

STANDFIRST: "Defence minister says non-nuclear principles should be revisited given the current global security 'crisis'"

BODY (verbatim as returned):
"Japan's defence minister renewed calls for opening a debate on acquiring nuclear weapons, saying Tokyo could not afford to rule out security options as tensions with China, Russia and North Korea continued to intensify."
"He argued that Japan should discuss its nuclear policy 'without taboos', including the possibility of revisiting its long-standing non-nuclear principles and of acquiring nuclear-powered submarines."
"Mr Koizumi said the government wasn't currently committing to any policy, but that options shouldn't be excluded before they were properly debated. At a press conference on Tuesday, he stressed the need to explain the changing security environment to the public, particularly as Japan was the only nation ever to suffer nuclear attacks in wartime."
"Mr Koizumi's comments come as the government prepares to revise three key national security documents by the end of the year. The review may include discussion of the nation's non-nuclear principles."
"Discussions are picking up in particular around the third principle, which prohibits Japan from allowing nuclear weapons to be introduced on its territory."
"Prime minister Sanae Takaichi said that Japan maintained the principles and reaffirmed commitment to a world without atomic weapons. But when asked whether the principles would be explicitly included in the three strategic documents due to be revised by the end of the year, she declined to comment."
"Mr Koizumi said earlier this month that Tokyo wasn't ruling out acquiring such vessels, shortly after a US navy official expressed support for the idea."

PEOPLE: Shinjiro Koizumi, Japanese Defence Minister. Sanae Takaichi, Prime Minister of Japan. Kazuyuki Yamazaki, Japan's ambassador to the UN. Antonio Guterres, UN Secretary-General. Stephen Nagy, professor of politics and international studies, International Christian University, Tokyo.

DIRECT QUOTES (verbatim as returned):
Antonio Guterres, UN Secretary-General, to a high-level meeting in New York on TUESDAY 29 Sep: "We meet at the most dangerous nuclear moment since the end of the Cold War." He warned that nuclear arsenals were being expanded and modernised, and cited the failure of the latest review conference of the Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons to reach a consensus. Also: "These are not abstract [risks]... They increase the risks of [arms] racing, escalation [and] catastrophic miscalculation" — NB this last quote is elided in the snippet; do NOT print it without recovering the full sentence.
Kazuyuki Yamazaki, Japan's ambassador to the UN: said Tokyo was committed to the Comprehensive Nuclear-Test-Ban Treaty and its early entry into force, and that Japan would continue its effort to pass the lessons of Hiroshima and Nagasaki to future generations.
Stephen Nagy, professor, International Christian University, Tokyo: "The world's only nation to suffer atomic bombing in war codified its 'nuclear allergy' into the Three Non-Nuclear Principles of 1967 - no possession, no production, no introduction of nuclear weapons, and positioned itself as the moral centre of the global disarmament movement."
Nagy: "That allergy is now showing signs of remission, and the cure has been administered not by Tokyo but by Beijing, Pyongyang, and Moscow."

RELATED SAME-DAY ITEM (approved carrier NOT yet found — flagged): Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun said on Wednesday 30 Sep that Japan is a non-nuclear-weapon state party to the NPT and that "there is no room for bargaining".
